source.title: The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review

paper.citation: Griffin A., Kenny I.C., Comyns T.M., Lyons M. The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2020;50(3):561-580. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01218-2.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What evidence links the acute:chronic workload ratio to injury in team sports, and which calculation method is most defensible for application? Participants: Athletes represented in 22 included articles. Sport and level: Team-sport cohorts across the included literature. Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Acute and chronic workload summarized through rolling-average or exponentially weighted models.
paper.tldr: Twenty-two articles met the inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality was 8, with a range of 5 to 9. The review reported associations between ACWR and non-contact injury but recommended its use only within a broader multifactorial monitoring system. ACWR may describe recent loading in relation to prior loading, but it should not be used as a traffic-light injury oracle.
paper.methods: Design: Systematic review. Exposure or intervention: Acute and chronic workload summarized through rolling-average or exponentially weighted models. Comparator: Different workload ratios, time windows, variables, and injury outcomes across studies. Measurements and outcomes: Non-contact injury and study-specific internal or external workload measures. Analysis: Six-database search, data extraction, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessment of cohort-study quality.
paper.findings: Twenty-two articles met the inclusion criteria; median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality was 8, with a range of 5 to 9. The review reported associations between ACWR and non-contact injury but recommended its use only within a broader multifactorial monitoring system. Both calculation models had support; the authors favored the exponentially weighted approach for sensitivity while noting that suitable windows and variables depend on the sport.
paper.limitations: The evidence base was observational and heterogeneous, so association should not be interpreted as proof that manipulating ACWR reduces injury. The authors called for work across more sports, time frames, both sexes, and combinations with other risk factors. Later methodological criticism should be read alongside this review before operational thresholds are adopted.
paper.practicalImplications: ACWR may describe recent loading in relation to prior loading, but it should not be used as a traffic-light injury oracle. Preserve the underlying daily load data, make calculation choices explicit, inspect context and uncertainty, and use the ratio as one descriptive signal among exposure, availability, symptoms, capacity, and schedule constraints.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, aCWR may describe recent loading in relation to prior loading, but it should not be used as a traffic-light injury oracle. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
